items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: And he had me listen especially to Count Basie, Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington.

ctx.x: What was your first exposure to music of the big band era. Was it through records and/or radio?

Through recordings and especially introduced to me by my older brother. I had a brother who was six years my senior. So when I was eight he was fourteen. And he had me listen to bands from eight years old on, and he was seventeen I guess I was however, six years younger. And he had me listen especially to Count Basie, Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington. And I zeroed in on those three, most particularly on Count Basie. And I just became a big band nut.
But somewhere along the line, the bop came into the picture.

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: All the big bands came through and played there, the well-known bands, Count Basie, Duke Ellington, Erskine Hawkins, et cetera.

ctx.x: My name is William Brower, Jr., interviewer. Sitting across from me is Franklin Benjamin Foster, informant, and recording this interview is Matt Watson, directing the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Program. It is September 24, 1998. We are commence an oral history/life history interview of Mr. Foster. I’d like to begin by asking you to establish for us the facts of your birth and family. If you would extend from that, talk a bit about your earliest recollections of the community in which you were raised.

I was born Frank Benjamin Foster the Third at 2:15 a.m., September 23rd, 1928, to Lillian Watts Foster and Frank B. Foster. My mother’s maiden name was Lillian Iona Watts. My mother and father were natives of South Carolina, my father from Greenville and my mother from Seneca. My father came north with the idea of

marrying a northern girl, and he ended up marrying this girl [laughs] from his home state. Cincinnati was I think the third largest city in Ohio, located in the southwest corner of the state and the hub, the musical hub of what’s referred to in that area as the tri-state area—Ohio, Indiana, and Kentucky. Cincinnati was a very culturally diverse town, principally resided in by people of German ancestry, and I suppose there was a large influx of blacks from the south.
